name: Chin-to-philtrum ratio

lead: The chin-to-philtrum ratio compares how tall the chin is with how long the philtrum, the groove between nose and upper lip, is. Looksmaxxing communities use it as a quick check of lower-face harmony: a short philtrum with a tall chin, or the reverse, is described as throwing the lower third out of balance.

The often-quoted benchmark is about 1:2, philtrum to chin, though sources define the points differently. Surgical literature discusses lower-third proportions more broadly, and forum users use the ratio to discuss genioplasty, lip lifts and jaw surgery.

paras: People photograph or measure the face from front on, mark the base of the nose, the lip line and the bottom of the chin, and compare the upper-lip segment with the chin segment. Forum members then discuss options for changing it: genioplasty to shorten or lengthen the chin, a lip lift to shorten the philtrum, or jaw surgery that changes the upper jaw position.

The ratio is a screening heuristic and is measured differently by different people, so results vary with photo angle and landmarks. Procedures discussed in connection with it are surgeries with their own risks. A surgeon's assessment weighs lip competence, bite and overall profile, not one ratio.

angle.text: People use the ratio to diagnose where the lower face looks out of proportion and to decide what to change. It guides conversations about chin height, lip lifts and jaw surgery.

lead: The chin-to-philtrum ratio compares the vertical height of the chin with the length of the philtrum, the vertical groove of the upper lip [1]. It is used in looksmaxxing communities as a shorthand for lower-third harmony.

Users on looksmax.org ask what ranges are acceptable, whether a short philtrum is ideal, and how to correct a mismatch [2][3]. In one thread, a poster with a short philtrum and a tall chin was told by a surgeon that maxillary downgrafting or a genioplasty could balance the ratio [2].

Published facial-proportion research uses related measures: one review describes the lower third divided into thirds for upper lip, lower lip and chin, with the upper lip roughly 30 percent and lower lip plus chin about 70 percent of lower facial height [4].
infobox: Genioplasty, lip lift, Le Fort I

paras: The philtrum is the groove running from the base of the nose to the upper lip [1]. The ratio sets the length of this segment against the chin. Sources differ: some define chin height from lower lip to chin, others from the stomion (lip junction) to menton, so quoted ideals vary.

Academic descriptions of the lower third give the upper lip about 30 percent of the lower face and the lip-and-chin segment about 70 percent, and describe the chin as roughly 70 percent of lower facial height [4].

Threads ask for acceptable ranges and why the ratio matters [5][6]. In one, the poster with a tall chin weighed a genioplasty to reduce vertical height against a bimaxillary plan; a reply said a short philtrum with normal midface ratios would suggest bimax with chin height reduction, though impossible to judge without photos [2]. Another poster with a short philtrum asked about non-surgical fixes and was told genioplasty could make the chin less tall and more forward [3][4].
No studies found on the chin-to-philtrum ratio itself. Related literature on lip and lower-face proportions exists [4].

lore.intro: Forum threads treat the ratio as a diagnostic for the lower third and a guide for surgery planning [2][4].
